learning_goal: Tell the radius from the ulna at either end, name the parts of each, and explain how the radius turns over the ulna at two joints to pronate and supinate the hand.

structures.name: right radius
structures.label: Radius
structures.narration: The lateral bone — the thumb side. Small at the elbow, broad at the wrist. It is the bone that carries the hand.

structures.name: right ulna
structures.label: Ulna
structures.narration: The medial bone — the little finger side. Broad at the elbow, small at the wrist. It is the bone that carries the elbow. The two are mirror images in shape: whatever one is big at, the other is small at.

structures.name: interosseous membrane of right forearm
structures.label: Interosseous membrane
structures.narration: A sheet between the two shafts. Its fibres run downwards and medially, from radius to ulna, so a force landing on the hand is passed from the radius up to the ulna and on to the humerus. It also divides the forearm into a flexor and an extensor compartment.

structures.name: right humerus
structures.label: Humerus
structures.narration: Two surfaces at its lower end: the pulley-shaped trochlea for the ulna, the round capitulum for the radius.

structures.name: right scaphoid
structures.label: Scaphoid
structures.narration: One of the two carpal bones that sit against the lower end of the radius.

structures.name: right lunate
structures.label: Lunate
structures.narration: The other one. Scaphoid and lunate meet the radius; neither of them meets the ulna.

structures.name: right supinator
structures.label: Supinator
structures.narration: Wraps round the upper radius from the ulna and the lateral epicondyle. It unwinds the radius — that is supination. The posterior interosseous nerve passes through it.

structures.name: long head of right biceps brachii
structures.label: Biceps brachii — long head
structures.narration: Biceps ends on the radial tuberosity, which sits on the medial side of the bone. Pulling on it spins the radius outwards, which is why biceps is the strongest supinator — and why you drive a screw in with the right hand.

structures.name: short head of right biceps brachii
structures.label: Biceps brachii — short head
structures.narration: The second head joins the same tendon, so it pulls on the same tuberosity.

structures.name: humeral head of right pronator teres
structures.label: Pronator teres — humeral head
structures.narration: From the medial epicondyle to the middle of the lateral surface of the radius. It drags the radius across the ulna.

structures.name: ulnar head of right pronator teres
structures.label: Pronator teres — ulnar head
structures.narration: The second head comes off the coronoid process of the ulna. The median nerve runs between the two.

structures.name: right pronator quadratus
structures.label: Pronator quadratus
structures.narration: A flat square joining the two bones just above the wrist. It is the prime pronator and it also holds the distal radioulnar joint together.

structures.label: Head of radius
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the radius and the humerus within the proximal 15% of the radius — the radial head turning on the capitulum (gap 4.85 mm); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: A shallow disc on top of a narrow neck. It spins on the capitulum and inside the annular ligament. In a small child a sharp pull on the arm slips it out of that ring — a pulled elbow.

structures.label: Radial tuberosity
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the radius and the long head of biceps brachii in the upper third of the radius — the biceps tendon insertion (gap 0.10 mm, 20.5 mm off the shaft axis); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The bump below the neck where biceps lands. It faces medially, so the tendon has to wind round the bone — that winding is what makes biceps a supinator.

structures.label: Ulnar notch of the radius
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the radius and the ulna within the distal 15% of the radius — the distal radioulnar joint (gap 1.45 mm); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: A hollow on the medial side of the lower radius. The head of the ulna sits in it, and the radius swings around that head in pronation.

structures.label: Styloid process of the radius
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME — the most distal point of the distal 12% of the radius, 41.7 mm off the shaft axis on the lateral side; see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The point you feel at the base of the thumb, in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. In life it reaches about a centimetre lower than the ulnar styloid; after a Colles fracture it no longer does, and that lost step is what you are checking for.

structures.label: Olecranon
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME — the most proximal point of the ulna, 34.0 mm off the shaft axis and 17.5 mm above the top of the radius; see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The point of the elbow, and the only part of the forearm you lean on. Triceps pulls on it, and it drops into the olecranon fossa when the elbow straightens.

structures.label: Trochlear notch
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the ulna and the humerus within the proximal 20% of the ulna — the notch gripping the trochlea (gap 0.62 mm); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: A deep C-shaped grip on the trochlea, between the olecranon behind and the coronoid process in front. This is the elbow joint proper — a hinge, and a very stable one.

structures.label: Coronoid process
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME — the most anterior point of the ulna between 78% and 95% of its height, 16.7 mm off the shaft axis; see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The front lip of the notch. Brachialis lands just below it, and the ulnar heads of pronator teres and flexor digitorum superficialis come off it.

structures.label: Radial notch of the ulna
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the ulna and the radius within the proximal 20% of the ulna — the proximal radioulnar joint (gap 1.67 mm); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: A small facet on the lateral side of the coronoid process. The radial head spins in it, held there by the annular ligament.

structures.label: Head of the ulna
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the ulna and the radius within the distal 15% of the ulna — the ulnar head in the ulnar notch of the radius (gap 1.45 mm); see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The ulna has its head at the bottom, the radius has its head at the top. The ulnar head does not reach the carpus — an articular disc hangs between it and the wrist bones.

structures.label: Styloid process of the ulna
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME — the most distal point of the distal 12% of the ulna, 30.5 mm off the shaft axis; see tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: A short peg off the back and medial side of the ulnar head. You can feel it on the back of your wrist below the little finger. Unlike the radial styloid it stays put while the hand turns.

views.title: Two bones, side by side
views.narration: The forearm has two bones lying side by side. With the palm facing forward, the radius is lateral and the ulna is medial. Everything else in this scene exists to explain how those two get along.

views.title: Which is which
views.narration: Learn them by their ends. The ulna is heavy at the top and thin at the bottom. The radius is thin at the top and heavy at the bottom. If a bone is broad where you are looking, you are at the elbow end of the ulna or the wrist end of the radius.

views.title: The elbow end
views.narration: At the elbow the ulna does the work. Its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus like a spanner, with the olecranon behind and the coronoid process in front. The radial head only rests against the capitulum.

views.title: The wrist end
views.narration: At the wrist the radius does the work. Scaphoid and lunate meet the radius alone; the ulna is kept off the carpus by an articular disc. So a fall on the outstretched hand loads the radius, and the radius is what breaks.

views.title: Joined in three places
views.narration: Three links hold the bones together: a pivot joint at the top, a pivot joint at the bottom, and the interosseous membrane in between. The two pivots always move together, because they are the two ends of the same turning axis.

views.title: The axis of rotation
views.narration: What is traced here is the radius itself, top to bottom: head, tuberosity, ulnar notch, styloid. The turning AXIS is the second line drawn, and it is not the same line — it runs from the centre of the radial head to the head of the ulna, cutting across the radius rather than along it. The radius spins on that axis at the top and swings around it at the bottom, which is why the hand turns but the elbow does not.

views.title: Pronation — the radius crosses over

ops.kind: pulls the radius round the ulna

views.narration: In pronation the radius rolls across the front of the ulna and the two bones cross. Pronator quadratus does it every time; pronator teres is added for speed and power. The ulna itself does not move.

views.title: Supination — unwinding it
views.narration: Supination unwinds the crossing. Supinator alone is enough for a slow turn; add force and biceps takes over, pulling on the radial tuberosity. Biceps only supinates well with the elbow bent, which is why you flex the elbow to open a stiff jar.

views.title: Cut across the middle
views.narration: Mid-shaft, both bones are triangular in section and face each other across a sharp interosseous border. The membrane strung between those borders is the wall that separates the flexors in front from the extensors behind.

views.title: Where they break
views.narration: Four names to keep, and every site named is lit. Colles: the lower radius breaks and the fragment tilts backwards — the dinner-fork wrist. Smith: the same break tilting forwards. Monteggia: the upper ulna breaks and the radial head dislocates. Galeazzi: the lower radius breaks and the distal radioulnar joint dislocates. In the last two, one bone breaking forces the other out of joint — because the two are a single ring.

gaps: The catalog's smallest unit is a whole radius and a whole ulna, so every named feature — olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear and radial notches, both styloid processes, the radial tuberosity, both heads — is a derived landmark anchor rather than its own model. Each was measured on the meshes by tools/derive-forearm-landmarks.mjs and carries the measurement that placed it; all TEN stay status:"needs-review" until a human clears them in-app. This note previously said eleven; the file has ten and always did.

The obvious eleventh landmark is the neck of the radius, which the head-of-radius narration names. It is not authored because it cannot be measured honestly with the two definitions tools/derive-landmark.mjs offers. A neck is defined by being the NARROWEST part of a bone, which is neither a contact nor an extreme. Tried 2026-08-29: contact between the radius and supinator converges to a 0.21 mm gap, but on a single witness, and it lands at w=0.81 — below the radial tuberosity at w=0.83, so it is upper shaft and not neck. Placing the anchor by eye between the head and the tuberosity would look measured and would not be, so it stays unauthored until either a neck mesh exists or the tool learns a minimum-cross-section definition.

Measured on these meshes the ulna reaches 0.8 mm further distally than the radial styloid, so the roughly 1 cm step by which the radial styloid normally lies below the ulnar styloid is NOT visible on the model. The narration teaches the relationship because it is what a Colles fracture abolishes, but a student must not read the offset off this scene. The same is true in the full-resolution and lite mesh sets, so it is the source segmentation, not the decimation.

There is no mesh for the annular ligament, the triangular fibrocartilage / articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint, the oblique cord or the elbow joint capsule, so the ligaments that actually hold these two pivots together are described rather than shown.

Pronation and supination are taught as before-and-after positions with the muscles that drive them. The renderer cannot animate the radius crossing the ulna, because that needs an articulated skeleton and BodyParts3D delivers static meshes.

No nerve or artery meshes exist for the upper limb, so the posterior interosseous nerve winding through supinator and the median nerve passing between the heads of pronator teres — both common exam questions and both reasons these bones matter clinically — are narration only.
